notes.meaning: Fourteen years later, Paul returned to Jerusalem with Barnabas and Titus. He brought Titus, an uncircumcised Gentile Christian, to show that Gentiles do not need Jewish rites to be accepted. He had labored independently for many years, proving he did not get his message from the Jerusalem leaders.

God directed Paul to go to Jerusalem by a special revelation, not because human leaders summoned him. He met privately with the chief apostles to explain what he was preaching to the Gentiles. This wise step prevented public arguments and protected his work from being ruined by misunderstandings.

Even though Titus was a Greek, the apostles in Jerusalem did not force him to be circumcised. Circumcision was the Jewish ritual sign of the covenant. By leaving Titus uncircumcised, the leaders agreed with Paul that Gentile believers do not have to keep the ceremonies of Moses.

Trouble began because false brothers sneaked into their company to spy on their freedom. These legalistic intruders wanted to force Gentile believers under the heavy rules of the Mosaic law. Paul knew that losing Christian freedom would lead to spiritual slavery for everyone.

Paul and Barnabas refused to give in to these false brothers even for a moment. Although Paul was often gentle about harmless customs, he stood firm here because the gospel itself was at stake. He fought to protect the true message of free grace for the Galatians and all Gentiles.

The prominent leaders in Jerusalem did not add anything new to Paul's message or authority. God does not judge people by outward titles, fame, or seniority. The apostles saw that Paul's teaching was already complete and given directly by God.

Instead of correcting Paul, the leaders recognized that God had given him the mission to the Gentiles, just as He had given Peter the mission to the Jews. The same Holy Spirit worked powerfully through Peter among the Jews and through Paul among the Gentiles. Both men preached the very same gospel to different audiences.

James, Peter, and John were respected as pillars, or strong supports, of the church. When they saw the grace God had given Paul, they shook hands with Paul and Barnabas in full fellowship. They agreed to divide their areas of work, sending Paul to the Gentiles and remaining focused on the Jews.

The Jerusalem leaders asked only one thing: that Paul remember the poor Christians living in Judea. Paul was already eager to do this, and he later collected money from Gentile churches to help them. Caring for those in need showed real love and kept Jewish and Gentile believers united in Christ.

Later, when Peter visited the city of Antioch, Paul had to confront him openly. Peter had acted wrongly and deserved blame for his behavior. Paul's public challenge proved that he was Peter's equal in apostolic authority and had to defend the truth of the gospel.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching holds that Peter remained the supreme head of the church, and that Paul rebuked Peter for his personal conduct and lack of firmness in discipline, not for error in definitive doctrine.

notes.meaning: At first, Peter freely shared meals with Gentile Christians, knowing God accepts them without the Jewish ceremonial law. But when some Jewish visitors arrived from Jerusalem, Peter became afraid of what they would say and pulled away. His fear of man caused him to abandon table fellowship with Gentile believers.

The other Jewish believers followed Peter's bad example and acted dishonestly as well. Tragically, even Barnabas, who had worked closely with Gentiles, was swept up in their hypocrisy. Hypocrisy means pretending to believe something while acting against what you know is true.

Paul saw that their actions did not walk in line with the true gospel. Because the offense was public and damaging the church, Paul rebuked Peter in front of everyone. He asked Peter how he could live like a Gentile in private, yet now pressure Gentiles to obey Jewish laws to be accepted.

Paul explains that even those born as Jews, who possessed God's law, could never be justified by keeping it. To be justified means to be declared righteous and right with God. Right standing before God comes only through faith in Jesus Christ, because human efforts to obey the law can never save anyone.

differ.view: Some Presbyterians emphasize that justification means God treats the believer as if he had never sinned on the ground of Christ's merits, rather than a literal transfer of moral character.

notes.meaning: Opponents objected that leaving the Jewish law to trust Christ alone makes people sinners, as if Christ promotes sin. Paul forcefully rejects this thought. Christ does not lead anyone to sin; He simply exposes the sin that was already there and calls us to trust His grace alone.

If a person leaves the law for Christ and then tries to rebuild that system of legal rules, he proves he is a lawbreaker. Going back to the law admits that abandoning it earlier was wrong. Going backward to earn God's favor by rule-keeping ruins the whole message of grace.

The law showed Paul his helplessness and spiritual failure, driving him to die to any hope of saving himself by it. By trusting Christ, the law's power to condemn him was broken forever. He died to the legal system so that he could be truly alive to God through new, spiritual devotion.

Paul explains that his old, self-centered self died on the cross with Christ. He now lives a transformed life because Jesus lives inside him by His Spirit. His daily earthly life is fueled by trust in the Son of God, who loved him personally and gave His life for him.

differ.view: Lutherans emphasize that faith joins the believer so completely to Christ that sin, death, and the devil are crucified, bringing peace to a terrified conscience apart from good works.

notes.meaning: Paul insists that he does not reject or make void God's gift of free grace. If people could make themselves righteous before God by obeying the law, then Jesus had no reason to die. Looking to our own moral efforts for salvation treats the cross of Christ as completely useless.
